To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the anomalous dispersion characteristics of superluminal (fast) light propagation and the normal dispersion characteristics of slow light propagation can be used to enhance absolute and relative rotation measurement, respectively.
(i) the sensitivity for absolute rotation can be greatly enhanced by use of fast light, and (ii) the sensitivity for relative rotation can be greatly improved by using slow light.

(1) anomalous dispersion can be used to enhance the sensitivity of a resonator-based absolute rotation sensor, and (2) normal dispersion can be used for relative rotation sensing in an Sagnac interferometric gyroscope.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of the group index to enhance the performance of optical gyroscopes.
the use of fast and slow light to enhance the sensitivity of a Sagnac interferometric gyroscope.
developing the physics of slow light for applications in rotation sensing, and with demonstrating the potential of slow light in enhancing rotation sensitivity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of slow light can enhance the sensitivity of rotation sensing, while the use of fast light can enhance the accuracy of rotation sensing.
slow light and superluminal light both have the potential to significantly enhance the sensitivity of rotation sensing.
the use of slow light in an active cavity can lead to a sensitivity enhancement factor of the order of 10{sup -4} for relative rotation sensing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the anomalous dispersion of the superluminal group velocity can be used to enhance the sensitivity of the Sagnac interferometers, while normal dispersion of the slow light can be used to improve the precision of the Sagnacs.
the use of slow light can improve rotation sensing in both the absolute and relative cases.
the sensitivity enhancement for both absolute and relative rotation measurements is given by the square of the slowing or the superluminal propagation factor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sensitivity enhancement of the resonator-based optical gyroscopes may be as large as the enhancement of the interferometric gyroscopes, but without the latter's need for a phase reference.
the use of fast light or slow light in optical gyroscopes is a promising avenue for improving the performance of these devices.

the use of anomalous dispersion in an optical gyroscope may be used to enhance the sensitivity of absolute rotation sensing by as much as six orders of magnitude, while the use of normal dispersion can be used to enhance relative rotation sensing by up to 100.
